title: A Different Kind of Orders
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 31 of 40
content:
Danse discovered hobbies the way he approached hostile territory: suspiciously.

The settlement east of Bravo needed help rebuilding a collapsed workshop. We arrived with tools, nails, and enough salvaged lumber to make the job possible.

By noon, Danse had organized six civilians into teams.

By one, he had invented a rotation schedule.

By two, the workshop owner told him if he used the phrase “operational efficiency” one more time she was going to hit him with a board.

Danse looked offended.

I laughed from the roof.

“You’re supposed to be holding that beam,” he called.

“I can laugh and hold.”

“Your grip is slipping.”

“It is not.”

“It is.”

The workshop owner shouted, “He’s right.”

“Traitor.”

Danse smiled.

That was becoming easier too.

After the walls were up, the settlers cooked dinner for everyone. Danse stood near the edge of the firelight looking uncertain.

He was good at work.

Celebration confused him.

I carried two bowls over.

“Sit.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“That an order?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t take orders from you.”

“Interesting. Sit anyway.”

He did.

We ate stew while someone played a battered guitar. Children chased each other around the pump. A dog slept beneath the table.

Danse watched everything.

“You look like you’re expecting an ambush.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re scanning rooftops.”

“Habit.”

“You’re allowed to stop.”

“For how long?”

“As long as you want.”

His spoon paused.

“That still feels strange.”

“What?”

“Wanting things without a reason.”

I thought about the list in his pocket.

“Try one.”

He frowned.

“One what?”

“One thing you want right now.”

Danse looked around.

His eyes landed on the guitar.

“That.”

I nearly smiled too obviously.

“You play?”

“No.”

“Want to?”

“I said I wanted the music.”

“Specificity matters.”

He gave me a look.

When the musician finished, I asked if Danse could try.

Danse looked betrayed.

“I didn’t agree to this.”

“You said you wanted it.”

“I said—”

The guitar was placed in his hands.

He stared at it like a live grenade.

The settlement went quiet.

“Outstanding,” I whispered.

Danse glared.

Then he tried one chord.

It sounded terrible.

A child laughed.

Danse looked at the child.

Then at me.

Then tried again.

By the fifth attempt he had something recognizable.

By the tenth he was smiling.

Not because he was good.

Because he was allowed to be bad.

That was new.

On the walk back to Bravo, he carried the borrowed guitar pick in his pocket.

“You enjoyed yourself,” I said.

“I tolerated the activity.”

“You smiled for twenty consecutive seconds.”

“Unverified.”

“I counted.”

“You need more hobbies.”

“So do you.”

He looked at me.

“What would you choose?”

“For you?”

“Yes.”

I thought.

“Something useless.”

His expression became suspicious.

“Why?”

“Because you’re very good at useful.”

“That sounds like a compliment.”

“It is.”

He waited for the criticism.

I let him wait.

Eventually he said, “And?”

“And nothing.”

He looked almost cheated.

I laughed.

Back at Bravo, Danse took the duty roster out of the drawer.

For a second I expected him to resurrect it.

Instead he flipped it over.

On the blank side he wrote:

LEARN THREE CHORDS.

I stood behind him.

“That an objective?”

“No.”

“A mission?”

“No.”

“An order?”

He looked over his shoulder.

“No.”

“What, then?”

Danse’s expression softened.

“Something I want.”

I kissed his cheek.

He turned red.

“Good answer.”

The guitar did not stay borrowed for long.

Three days later the workshop owner arrived at Bravo carrying it beneath one arm.

Danse opened the bunker door and stared.

“I thought you needed this.”

She shrugged. “Got another one. This one sounds terrible.”

“It sounded terrible because I was playing it.”

“That too.”

She handed it to him.

Danse did not take it.

“What do you want for it?”

“Nothing.”

His expression hardened automatically.

“I don’t accept equipment without fair trade.”

“It’s not equipment, soldier.”

His jaw tightened at the title even though she had not meant anything by it.

The woman noticed.

“Sorry. Danse.”

He looked at the guitar again.

“Why give it to me?”

“Because you looked like you wanted it and tried very hard not to.”

I made the mistake of smiling.

Danse pointed at me without looking away from her.

“Do not.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

The woman laughed and pushed the guitar into his hands.

“You fixed my roof. Call it even.”

“That was already compensated.”

“Then call it a gift.”

Danse looked genuinely trapped.

I had seen him face super mutants with less concern.

Finally he said, “Thank you.”

No qualification.

No promise to repay.

Progress.

That evening he sat outside Bravo with the guitar balanced awkwardly against one thigh.

I joined him with two bottles of beer.

“Three chords?”

“Two and a half.”

“What is half a chord?”

“The third one is inconsistent.”

He demonstrated.

It buzzed horribly.

I winced.

“Honest feedback?”

“No.”

“It sounds like a molerat being strangled.”

“I specifically said no.”

He adjusted his fingers and tried again.

Better.

Not good.

Better.

“You know,” I said, “you don’t have to improve every time you touch it.”

“That defeats the purpose of practice.”

“Sometimes the purpose is doing something because you enjoy doing it badly.”

He stopped.

“That is irrational.”

“Yes.”

“Why would anyone enjoy incompetence?”

“Because there’s no consequence.”

Danse looked at the strings.

I let the words sit.

Most things he had learned badly could kill someone.

Marksmanship. Patrol procedure. Power armor. Field medicine. Command.

A missed guitar chord harmed nothing except local wildlife.

He tried the terrible chord again.

It buzzed.

This time he laughed.

“That,” I said. “Exactly that.”

He shook his head.

“You’re very pleased with yourself.”

“Constantly.”

“Unjustifiably.”

“Also constantly.”

Danse took a drink.

Then he held the guitar out to me.

“Your turn.”

“I never said I could play.”

“You criticize with confidence.”

“That is unrelated to expertise.”

“I’ve noticed.”

I took the guitar and produced a sound so bad he stared at me.

“Was that intentional?”

“No.”

“Outstanding.”

We spent an hour being awful together.

When darkness settled over the field, Danse leaned back on his hands.

“I had hobbies before the Brotherhood,” he said.

I waited.

“At Rivet City. Cutler and I collected old holotapes. Music, mostly. We’d trade scrap for anything that still played.”

“You remembered that?”

“I always remembered. I just didn’t think of it as important.”

“What happened to the tapes?”

“Lost. Sold. Some probably went with him when…”

He stopped.

The grief arrived without flattening the whole evening.

That was new too.

“What did you listen to?”

“Anything. Jazz. Classical. Terrible pre-War advertisements.”

I smiled.

“So useless things were in you the whole time.”

Danse frowned.

“I dislike your phrasing.”

“Because I’m right?”

“Because you sound smug.”

I handed the guitar back.

The first lesson lasted twenty-three minutes before Danse attempted to create a practice schedule.

“No.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You reached for the paper.”

“I was going to record the chord shapes.”

“With times.”

“Possibly.”

I confiscated the pencil.

Danse glared at me and tried the chord again.

It buzzed.

His jaw tightened.

“Again,” he said.

“Not until you say one nice thing about the mistake.”

“That is ridiculous.”

“Then we’re done.”

He stared at the guitar as if it had joined a conspiracy.

Finally: “It did not injure anyone.”

“Beautiful.”

“It demonstrated incorrect finger pressure.”

“That’s almost healthy.”

“It sounded terrible.”

“You were doing so well.”

Danse sighed.

Then he played the chord wrong again, less carefully this time.

The buzz filled the room.

Nothing exploded. No one died. No report would record it.

He looked at me.

“That is… strangely irritating.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because you’re allowed to be bad at something long enough to become better.”

Danse considered that with more seriousness than the sentence deserved.

Then he tried again.

The second lesson happened outside because Danse decided the bunker walls were “acoustically punitive.”

I suspected he simply did not want me laughing where the sound echoed.

He practiced until his fingertips reddened.

“Stop.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re bleeding.”

He looked offended by his own hand.

“This instrument is poorly designed.”

“Millions of dead musicians disagree.”

“They are unavailable for questioning.”

I took the guitar from him and handed him a strip of cloth.

Danse wrapped two fingertips, stared at the strings, and said, “Tomorrow.”

I nearly applauded.

He noticed.

“Don’t.”

“You voluntarily stopped before finishing.”

“I am capable of restraint.”

“Historic event.”

He kissed me to end the commentary.

A breeze moved through the grass. Danse adjusted his grip, not because anyone was grading him, but because he wanted the next sound to be better than the last.

He played the half-chord again.

It rang clean.

Danse blinked.

“There.”

I grinned.

“Three.”

His smile arrived slowly.

“Three.”

Then he deliberately put one finger in the wrong place and made it buzz again.

I stared.

Danse looked innocent.

“What?”

“You did that on purpose.”

“Unverified.”

I laughed.

He was learning how to fail harmlessly.

That might have been the strangest kind of freedom yet.
